iac-and-hcl-basics.r: A server was configured by hand and nobody could recreate it after it failed. Describing it in Terraform meant the next one was created from code in minutes, and every change was reviewed.
iac-and-hcl-basics.x: Infrastructure as code gives repeatability and review, but only if the code is the only way changes happen. Decide how you handle emergency manual changes and how you reconcile them.

providers-and-resources.r: A resource was created before the network it depended on, and the apply failed halfway. Referencing the network's output made the dependency explicit, so Terraform created things in the right order.
providers-and-resources.x: Dependencies should be expressed through references, not hidden assumptions. Pin provider versions, read provider upgrade notes and be careful with lifecycle rules that can destroy data.

variables-and-outputs.r: A module accepted a free-form string for the instance size, and someone typed a size that did not exist. Adding a validation rule gave a clear error at plan time instead of a failure midway through apply.
variables-and-outputs.x: Inputs are your module's interface. Type them, validate them, give sensible defaults, and keep outputs minimal and stable, since changing them breaks every caller.

expressions-and-dynamic-blocks.r: Resources were created with count, and removing one item from the middle of the list made Terraform want to replace several others. Switching to for_each keyed by name made each resource stable.
expressions-and-dynamic-blocks.x: Choose keys that do not change. Prefer for_each with meaningful keys over count with positions, and keep expressions readable, since clever code is hard to review at plan time.

state.r: Two engineers applied at the same time without locking and the state file was corrupted. A remote backend with locking and versioning prevented a repeat and allowed a rollback of the state.
state.x: State is sensitive and critical: it may hold secrets and it defines what Terraform believes exists. Protect it with access control, encryption, locking and backups, and restrict who can run state commands.

modules.r: A module was changed in place and every environment that used it changed at the next apply. Versioning the module and upgrading each environment on purpose let the team test changes first.
modules.x: Modules are shared APIs. Keep them small and focused, version them, avoid deep nesting and write down what is stable. Too many options create a wrapper nobody understands.

secrets-and-sensitive-data.r: A database password marked sensitive was still stored in plain text in the state file, which a wider group could read. Moving the password to a secrets manager and restricting access to state closed the gap.
secrets-and-sensitive-data.x: Sensitive flags only hide output. Assume state contains secrets, generate or fetch them at runtime where possible, and encrypt and restrict state. Rotate anything that was ever in code.

aws-and-azure-end-to-end.r: The same web stack was built on two clouds, and the differences were mostly in names, not ideas: network, load balancer, compute and database. Learning the pattern once made the second cloud much faster.
aws-and-azure-end-to-end.x: Concepts transfer, details do not. Resist hiding real differences behind a lowest common denominator module, and decide which parts truly need to be portable.

workflows-and-drift.r: A weekly plan showed a security group had been changed by hand to open a port. The plan highlighted the drift, the team reverted it and then added an alert so such changes were noticed sooner.
workflows-and-drift.x: Run plan on a schedule to detect drift, review plans before apply, and apply from one place. Decide in advance when drift is reverted and when code is updated to match.

testing-terraform.r: A small change removed a required tag, and a policy check in CI failed the pull request before anything reached the cloud. The same check later blocked an overly open firewall rule.
testing-terraform.x: Test at several levels: format, validate, lint, policy and, for critical modules, real deploy tests in a sandbox account. Balance cost and confidence, and run the cheap checks on every change.

environments-and-team-workflows.r: Workspaces were used to separate staging and production in one folder, and an engineer applied to production while thinking they were in staging. Separate directories and accounts per environment made that mistake much harder.
environments-and-team-workflows.x: Separate environments by account, state and credentials, not by habit. Make the target obvious, restrict production applies to a pipeline and keep differences between environments small and visible.

import-refactor-and-moved-blocks.r: A resource was renamed in code and Terraform planned to destroy and recreate it, which would have deleted a database. A moved block told Terraform it was the same object, and the plan showed no change.
import-refactor-and-moved-blocks.x: Read every plan for destroys. Use moved blocks and import with care, take a state backup before refactoring and test the plan in a copy when the object holds data.

large-configurations-and-performance.r: One huge configuration took twenty minutes to plan and any change risked everything. Splitting it into stacks by lifecycle and ownership made plans fast and kept mistakes local.
large-configurations-and-performance.x: Split by blast radius and rate of change, not by resource type. Manage dependencies between stacks explicitly, and avoid a single state that every team must touch.

debugging-terraform.r: An apply failed with a vague provider error. Turning on debug logs showed the cloud API rejected the request because of a quota, and raising the quota fixed it. A stale state lock was cleared only after confirming nobody was running an apply.
debugging-terraform.x: Read the plan and the provider error before changing anything. Check quotas, permissions and API limits, and never force-unlock without knowing who holds the lock.
